content: The extent of tumour resection is considered a critical prognostic factor in neuro-oncology. Image-guided surgery employs various advanced tools and technologies to enhance the precision of tumour removal. However, it remains uncertain whether these tools, some of which are highly expensive, should be routinely recommended as part of standard care for patients with brain tumours. This study aimed to evaluate whether image-guided surgery improves the extent of tumour resection compared to surgery without image guidance and to determine if any specific tool or technology is more effective. The primary objective was to compare the extent of tumour resection achieved with image-guided surgery versus surgery without image guidance or surgery using different image-guidance tools. Secondary outcomes included adverse events, overall survival (OS), progression-free survival (PFS), and quality of life (QoL). The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, and EMBASE, up to March 2013. They also reviewed reference lists of identified studies, hand-searched two neuro-oncology journals, and contacted neuro-oncologists, trial authors, and manufacturers for information on ongoing or unpublished trials. The study included patients of all ages with presumed new or recurrent brain tumours, diagnosed through clinical examination and imaging (CT, MRI, or both). Image-guidance interventions evaluated included intraoperative MRI (iMRI), fluorescence-guided surgery using 5-aminolevulinic acid (5-ALA), neuronavigation (including diffusion tensor imaging, DTI), and ultrasonography. Only randomised controlled trials (RCTs) were included, comparing surgery with and without image guidance or comparing different image-guidance tools. Subgroups included high-grade gliomas, low-grade gliomas, brain metastases, skull base meningiomas, and sellar or parasellar tumours. Two independent reviewers assessed the relevance of search results, critically appraised the studies, and extracted data using a predefined protocol. Four RCTs were identified, each evaluating a different image-guidance technique: iMRI (58 patients), 5-ALA fluorescence-guided surgery (322 patients), neuronavigation (45 patients), and DTI-neuronavigation (238 patients). Meta-analysis was not feasible due to differences in tumour locations (eloquent versus non-eloquent areas) and variations in the control arms, which often included selective use of neuronavigation. All studies had significant risk of bias, particularly the study on DTI-neuronavigation. The studies primarily included patients with high-grade gliomas, with one study also including low-grade gliomas. The extent of tumour resection was improved with iMRI (risk ratio [RR] for incomplete resection: 0.13, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.02 to 0.96, low-quality evidence), 5-ALA (RR: 0.55, 95% CI: 0.42 to 0.71), and DTI-neuronavigation (RR: 0.35, 95% CI: 0.20 to 0.63, very low-quality evidence). There was insufficient data to assess the impact of neuronavigation on the extent of resection. Adverse event reporting was incomplete, with evidence of significant reporting bias. While overall adverse events were low, there was concern that 5-ALA-guided surgery might lead to more frequent early neurological deficits. There was no clear evidence of improved overall survival with 5-ALA (hazard ratio [HR]: 0.82, 95% CI: 0.62 to 1.07) or DTI-neuronavigation (HR: 0.57, 95% CI: 0.32 to 1.00) in patients with high-grade gliomas. Progression-free survival data were unavailable in a format suitable for analysis. Quality of life data were reported in only one study, which suffered from significant attrition bias. In conclusion, there is low to very low-quality evidence, based on GRADE criteria, that image-guided surgery using iMRI, 5-ALA, or DTI-neuronavigation increases the proportion of patients with high-grade gliomas achieving complete tumour resection on postoperative MRI. There is a theoretical concern that maximising the extent of resection may increase the risk of adverse events, but this was poorly reported in the included studies. The effects of image-guided surgery on survival and quality of life remain unclear. Further research, including studies on ultrasound-guided surgery, is necessary to better understand the benefits and risks of these technologies.
